headline: Corsair's RM1000e (2026) PSU features ThermalProtect 12V-2x6 cable, preventing GPU connector melting at 65°C
summary: The new Corsair RM1000e (2026) power supply introduces a temperature-sensing 12V-2x6 cable that automatically shuts down GPU power if the connector reaches 65°C, aiming to prevent melting issues.
details: The Corsair RM1000e (2026) power supply, priced at $179.99 with a 7-year warranty, features a new ThermalProtect 12V-2x6 cable. This cable is designed to cut GPU power if its connector reaches 65°C, preventing potential melting. It offers strong efficiency, ripple, and regulation.

Corsair, a company with decades of experience in PC components, has been selling PSUs for nearly two decades. They often commission platforms from OEMs but significantly alter them for improved performance and reliability. Their RMe line is a mainstream series, now in its latest revision.

The 2026 RMe units, launched August 18th, ship with the new ThermalProtect 12V-2x6 cable, a 600W cable with a built-in temperature sensor. This hardware solution directly addresses the notorious melting connector problem. The unit also boasts a Cybenetics Platinum efficiency rating.

The PSU comes in Corsair's signature yellow-and-black box, highlighting ATX 3.1, PCIe 5.1, 12V-2x6, and "Nvidia 50 Series Ready" certifications. However, the bundle is minimal, including only an AC cord, mounting screws, zip ties, and a basic booklet, which feels stingy for its $180 price point.

ThermalProtect's sensor is located within the cable comb, 30mm from the graphics card connector. If the temperature hits 65°C, it signals the card to shut down in milliseconds, resulting in a black screen while the rest of the system remains operational. This is a hardware-based solution requiring no software.

headline: Fair Work Commission condemns 'plain wrong' AI legal advice, citing 40% case surge
summary: Australia's Fair Work Commission has seen a 40% rise in cases, partly due to litigants using AI, leading to new disclosure rules and a landmark $1,230 fine for one applicant.
details: Australia's Fair Work Commission (FWC) has condemned "plain wrong" AI legal advice, noting a 40% surge in cases partly attributed to litigants using generative AI. This has prompted the FWC to implement new rules requiring applicants to disclose AI use from October 20.

One notable case involved former ALDI worker Sadnan Khan, who was ordered to pay $1,230 towards ALDI's legal fees. The FWC found he used AI as a "quasi-legal advisor" despite repeated warnings that his case had no substantial prospects of success.

Khan stated he used a paid version of ChatGPT to understand legal cases cited by the tribunal and ALDI, admitting comprehension barriers affected his prompts. He plans to use "two or three" different AI agents for his appeal.

While the FWC criticized Khan's misuse, it acknowledges AI's potential to improve access to justice for applicants with genuine claims. It clarified that AI use is not inherently problematic when approached critically as "one tool among many."

In contrast, Macquarie University lecturer Gregory Baker successfully challenged casual employment laws using a team of AI agents. He treated his claim as a "software development project," ensuring logical coherence and correct citations.

Baker's success highlights the potential for sophisticated AI use in legal matters, but he also warned about a potential five-year gap between advanced, paid AI and free, less sophisticated models, which could exacerbate inequality in access to effective AI tools.
